articles.title: Our example env file documents 19 variables, the code reads 15 of them, and its longest comment describes a design we deleted
articles.description: .env.example is the first file a new contributor opens and the last file anybody updates. PubTrivia has two of them, one for the Next.js app that serves the marketing site and the dashboard and one for the WebSocket server that runs the live half of a quiz night, and I went through both against every process.env read in the repository. The root file documents 19 variables. Fifteen of them are read by the app's own source. Here is the gap, in both directions. Four documented, never read $ comm -23 documented.txt read.txt GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET NEXTJS_INTERNAL_URL NEXT_PUBLIC_STRIPE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN Four variables, four different reasons, and only one of them is a mistake. GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET is never read because this app does not perform the OAuth exchange. Supabase does, and the secret is pasted into Supabase's dashboard. It is in our example file so that somebody setting the project up knows they need one, which is a reasonable thing for an example file to do and a slightly odd thing for an example file to do, since nothing will ever read the value they put there. NEXTJS_INTERNAL_URL is read by the other package. It is in the root file with a note saying exactly that, in capital letters: # NOTE: this variable is READ BY THE WS SERVER, not by Next.js itself. # Set it in ws-server/.env (or ws-server/.env.local) alongside WS_INTERNAL_SECRET. # It is documented here to clarify the distinction from the other WS variables above. That comment exists because three of the four variables with WS in the name are read by Next.js and this one is not, which is confusing enough to have been written down twice. SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN is read during the build by the Sentry webpack plugin, not by any line of our code. A variable can be essential and still never appear in your source. NEXT_PUBLIC_STRIPE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY is the mistake. It is a leftover from an earlier approach where Stripe's hosted pricing table rendered the plans. That element is gone, the key is read by nothing, and the script tag that would have used it is still in the root layout: <Script src="https://js.stripe.com/v3/pricing-table.js" strategy="lazyOnload" /> I wrote a correction post about that script a while back after measuring it on the live site, and it is still there, still loading on every page, still defining a custom element that no page uses. The example file is the second artifact keeping a deleted design alive. Two read, never documented $ comm -13 documented.txt read.txt NEXT_RUNTIME NODE_ENV Both are provided by the framework. NODE_ENV gates whether lib/site.ts treats the deployment as the production site, which decides whether pages are indexable and whether the Organization JSON-LD is emitted. NEXT_RUNTIME is read twice in instrumentation.ts to decide which Sentry config to load. Neither belongs in an example file, because writing them there would invite somebody to set them by hand. A credential used as a boolean The one variable whose read surprised me is GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID. It appears in exactly one file, and it is never passed to anything: Its presence decides whether the "Continue with Google" button renders. Its value is unused, because, as above, the exchange happens in Supabase. So an OAuth client id, the single least secret credential in any OAuth setup, is functioning here as a feature flag, and the feature it flags is configured in a different product's dashboard. It works, and I half want to replace it with GOOGLE_SIGNIN_ENABLED=true so the next person does not spend a minute wondering where the id goes. Four of the 19 names carry the NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix, which in Next.js means "inline this into the JavaScript the browser downloads". Three of them really are in the client bundle: the Supabase project URL and its anon key, which are designed to be public and protected by row level security, and the WebSocket URL a phone has to connect to. The fourth, the Stripe publishable key, is public by design too and is not in the bundle because nothing reads it. The thing worth checking in your own project is not whether the prefix is there, it is whether anything without the prefix has quietly been handed to a client component. The longest comment in the file is out of date This is the finding I actually care about. The entry for MANAGED_PAYMENTS_ENABLED carries a twenty-line comment, the longest in the file, and the last third of it describes a design that no longer exists: # Because our line items use a pre-created Price id, the accompanying tax # settings live on the Stripe objects and must also be set there: tax_code # txcd_10103000 on each Product, tax_behavior "exclusive" on each Price. There are no Products. There are no Prices. We deleted them, and every Checkout line item is now built inline from one table of local amounts, which is the whole reason the figure on the pricing page is the figure on the card. The code that the comment is about says so itself: So the repository contains two documents about the same tax setting, 60 lines apart in different files, and they disagree about where it lives. Anybody following the example file would go into the Stripe Dashboard looking for Products to annotate, find none, and conclude the setup was incomplete. A stale comment in an example file is worse than no comment, because its tone is instructional. The other half of that entry is still exactly right and worth keeping as a pattern: # Master switch, MoR is applied only when this is exactly "true", and even then # only for the EU-27 countries listed in utils/stripe/managed-payments.ts === 'true' rather than truthiness, which means MANAGED_PAYMENTS_ENABLED=1 and MANAGED_PAYMENTS_ENABLED=yes both leave it off. For a flag that changes who the merchant of record is on a real invoice, refusing to guess is the correct amount of pedantry. The second file, and the variable in neither The WebSocket server has its own example file with six entries, and the two halves of the system have almost nothing in common. One variable, DATABASE_URL, appears in both. The shared secret appears in both under the same name. And then the conventions diverge: Concern Next.js app WS server Redis UPSTASH_REDIS_REST_URL + _TOKEN REDIS_URL Redis client Upstash REST ioredis Redis needed? yes, for rate limits no, only for multi-instance fan-out Port n/a WS_PORT, or PORT The Redis split is deliberate: a REST client works in the edge runtime where a TCP one does not, and the WS server has no such constraint. The port line is the interesting one, because the variable the production server actually listens on is documented in neither example file: PORT is injected by the host. It is in no example file, it is in no dashboard field anybody typed, and it is the one that is actually in use in production. The error message is the only place in the repository that tells you so, which is a decent argument for writing fallbacks into error strings rather than comments: the string is the one piece of documentation that gets read at the moment it matters. What I am changing Three things, all small. Delete NEXT_PUBLIC_STRIPE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY and the pricing-table script together, since neither has a job. Rewrite the last paragraph of the Managed Payments comment to say where the tax code actually rides. Rename the Google variable to the flag it is. The broader lesson is that an example env file is a test with no runner. Nothing in a build fails when it drifts, and the drift here was not a missing variable, which somebody would hit immediately. It was four surplus names and one confident paragraph about objects that no longer exist. The check is twenty seconds of comm over two sorted lists, and it is worth running the day after any refactor that touches a third-party integration. See the result rather than the config The part of this that a reader can actually verify is the pricing: The pricing page builds its figures from one table of local amounts, the same table Checkout builds its line items from. Load it through a VPN exit in another country and the currency changes with it. The features index and the solutions pages are the surfaces that NODE_ENV quietly governs, since it decides whether they are indexable at all. The free tier needs no card, so you can sign up and see the Google button whose existence is decided by whether a variable is set.

articles.title: GhostTales AI
articles.description: GhostTales AI – Where Every Story Has a Ghost This is my submission for the "Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine" (https://dev.to/challenges/hacktoberfest-week4-2026-10-26). What I Built I built GhostTales AI, an AI-powered spooky story generator inspired by the mysterious world of ghosts, Halloween and supernatural storytelling. The idea was to create an interactive experience where anyone can turn a simple idea into an immersive spooky story. Users can choose between three categories: Horror, Mystery and Supernatural. They can generate stories and enjoy them through a dedicated reading experience. Some of the features include: AI-powered spooky story generation. Multiple story categories. Immersive reading experience with word count and estimated reading time. Read Aloud functionality. Ambient background audio. Adjustable text size. Options to copy and generate another story. I wanted to make something that combines storytelling, creativity and AI in an engaging way. Demo 🔗 Live Demo: https://ghosttales-ai.ai.studio Code 💻 GitHub Repository: https://github.com/pieray2/GhostTales-AI How I Built It I built GhostTales AI using Google AI Studio. The project uses Google's Gemma open-weight model for AI-powered story generation. The application displays the Gemma model "gemma-4-26b-a4b-it". The frontend provides an interactive storytelling interface, while the AI integration generates stories based on the user's selected category and idea. I focused on creating a smooth experience with a visually immersive Halloween-inspired design. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? Open innovation makes AI development more flexible and accessible. Using an open-weight model like Gemma gives developers more freedom to explore AI, experiment with different models and build applications without depending entirely on a single closed AI provider. For GhostTales AI, Gemma provides the foundation for its storytelling experience and makes model choice and future experimentation possible. It also opens opportunities for developers to improve, adapt and extend projects as open AI technology evolves. My Agent Session Optional – Add your DevRelay agent session link here if available. The Spirit of It What if a machine could tell you a story that gives you chills? That was the inspiration behind GhostTales AI. I wanted to bring a little mystery into the digital world and turn ordinary ideas into stories that feel like they came from somewhere beyond the screen. Sometimes, the best stories are the ones that make you wonder what happens when the lights go out. 👻 Prize Categories No specific partner category claimed .

articles.title: Our test suite has no DOM: 266 tests in 603 milliseconds, and the two components it checks are rendered to a string
articles.description: PubTrivia is a Next.js app with 201 .tsx files, 52 of which are client components, and a test suite that cannot render a single one of them in a browser-like environment. There is no jsdom, no happy-dom, no Testing Library, and nothing in package.json that would provide one: $ grep -c 'jsdom\|happy-dom\|testing-library' package.json 0 The config is eleven lines: export default defineConfig({ test: { environment: 'node', include: ['**/__tests__/**/*.test.ts'], setupFiles: ['./__tests__/setup.ts'], }, resolve: { alias: { '@': path.resolve(__dirname, '.') } }, }) Two details in there decide the shape of everything else. environment: 'node' means there is no document. And the include pattern ends in .test.ts, so a file named Something.test.tsx would not be collected at all: it would sit in the repository looking like a test and never run. Here is what the suite actually contains, straight from vitest list: File Tests pricing/display-currency.test.ts 43 pricing/price-copy.test.ts 28 billing/managed-payments.test.ts 27 billing/checkout-route.test.ts 26 billing/checkout-session.test.ts 22 content/registry.test.ts 21 seed-data.test.ts 20 scoring.test.ts 16 gameplay.integration.test.ts 13 billing/stripe-webhook.test.ts indexnow.test.ts 10 maintenance.test.ts 9 routes.test.ts 8 server-clock.test.ts 5 content/page-metadata.test.ts 3 shared-constants.test.ts 2 266 tests, 16 files, 3,201 lines. Thirteen of them need a database. The other 253 need nothing: Test Files 15 passed (15) Tests 253 passed (253) Duration 603ms Four of the sixteen files call vi.mock, and twelve mock nothing, because there is nothing to mock: they import a module and call it. Technique one: render the component to a string anyway The interesting file is pricing/price-copy.test.ts, which has an actual React component under test. With no DOM, it reaches for the server renderer: import { createElement, type ComponentProps, type ComponentType } from 'react' import { renderToStaticMarkup } from 'react-dom/server' import PricingCards from '@/components/PricingCards' renderToStaticMarkup works fine in Node, so the component renders, wrapped in the same currency provider the real app wraps it in, once per currency in a list of six. Then the markup is thrown away and only the words survive, because what these tests assert is a promise about the pricing page: a visitor is charged the local figure they are shown, so no price surface may describe that figure as an approximation or a conversion from pounds. That is a list of banned phrases checked against the rendered text, and a regex over the visible text is exactly the right instrument for it. The limits are real. Nothing here can click. No test in this repository has ever fired an event, checked a focus ring, or asserted that a dialog closes. For a suite whose job is to protect money and metadata that is a defensible trade, but it should be said out loud rather than discovered later. Technique two: read the page as text Two files do not import the thing they test at all. The page metadata test regexes export const metadata out of 100 route files because importing one boots Supabase, and the price copy test does the same thing for the pages that read the request: The pricing cards are rendered for real; the pages that can't be rendered outside Next (they read the request, or pull in Supabase) are read as source, as __tests__/content/page-metadata.test.ts does. A third file, shared-constants.test.ts, parses a different package's source with a regex, because the WebSocket server is a separate build root that this test run cannot import from. Three files, then, that test code by reading it rather than running it. That is usually a smell, and here it is the consequence of one decision: the test runner is plain Node, so anything that only exists inside the Next.js runtime has to be checked some other way or not at all. The thirteen tests that need the world gameplay.integration.test.ts is the only file that reaches a service, and it is the longest in the suite at 543 lines for 13 tests. It gets its connection string from the setup file, which is seven lines: import { config } from 'dotenv' config({ path: '.env.local' }) So the entire difference between a unit test and an integration test in this repository is whether the file happens to import @/utils/db/db. There is no separate project, no tag, no testNamePattern in a second script. pnpm test runs all sixteen files, and the thirteen tests at the end of it write rows into a real Postgres. They are careful about it: every row the file creates is tracked and deleted in afterAll. But "deleted in afterAll" has a well-known failure mode, which is that you press Ctrl-C. An interrupted run leaves its rows behind, and the next thing to read that database sees them. If I were starting this suite again, the integration file would live behind its own script and its own database, and pnpm test would mean the 253 that need nothing. Two dependencies nothing imports While counting, two entries in devDependencies turned out to have no call sites at all: $ grep -rln "fast-check" app lib utils components __tests__ scripts ws-server/src $ grep -c coverage package.json 1 fast-check is a property-based testing library, imported by zero files. It was installed for the currency rounding work, which is the obvious candidate for generative tests (43 tests over six currencies, all of them hand-written examples), and then never used. @vitest/coverage-v8 is installed, and the single mention of the word "coverage" in package.json is that dependency line: there is no test:coverage script and no coverage block in the Vitest config, so no coverage report has ever been generated. I know the suite's size and its speed, and I genuinely do not know what fraction of the codebase it touches. The honest summary of our quality gates is shorter than it should be. pnpm test works and takes 603 milliseconds. pnpm format:check reports style issues in 335 files. pnpm lint has not run since the Next 16 upgrade, because next lint was removed and the command now reads its argument as a directory: $ pnpm lint $ next lint Invalid project directory provided, no such directory: /Users/daniel/Documents/programs/pub-trivia/lint And there is no .github directory in the repository, so nothing runs any of it except me, on this laptop, when I remember. Vercel builds and deploys on push without running a single test. What I am doing about it In order, cheapest first: split the integration file out of the default run, add the coverage script that the already-installed dependency makes free, and fix the lint script. None of that needs a new dependency. Adding jsdom is the one I keep not doing, and the reason is the same one that produced this shape in the first place. The things most likely to break on this site are a price in the wrong currency, a page that drops out of the sitemap, and a plan change that leaves somebody with no subscription. All three are testable in Node, in milliseconds, with no DOM. The dialog animation is not what keeps me up. See the surface these tests protect The 28 copy tests are all about one page, so the fastest way to see what they are guarding is to open it: The pricing page renders the plan cards that renderToStaticMarkup renders in the test, in your own currency, chosen from where the request comes from. Switch on a VPN and reload, and the figure changes while the wording around it does not. That invariance is what the tests exist for. The features index and the guides are built from the content registry that registry.test.ts checks with 21 assertions. The free tier needs no card, so you can sign up and look at the half of the app that has no tests at all.

articles.title: Your coding agent's sandbox is off. Here's how to turn it on without breaking everything.
articles.description: Every major coding agent now ships a sandbox. Claude Code has /sandbox, Codex has workspace-write, and there's Anthropic's open-source sandbox-runtime, nono and others. They all work the same way: deny everything, then allow what you list. And that is exactly why most people don't use them. The empty allowlist problem A deny-by-default sandbox asks you a question you can't answer up front: which websites and folders does my work need? So you switch it on and find out the hard way. npm install can't reach the registry. The dev server can't open a port. pip can't write its cache. git push can't read your SSH key. Each failure is either a permission prompt or a broken command. After an hour you either turn the sandbox off or add broad rules ("allow all of ~") that quietly undo it. The answer is already on your disk Claude Code saves a transcript of every session in ~/.claude/projects, and Codex does the same in ~/.codex/sessions. Every command your agent ran is in there. That history is the allowlist. You just need to read it carefully. What "carefully" means A transcript shows npm install, not that npm talked to registry.npmjs.org and wrote to ~/.npm. Turning commands into needs takes three things: A real shell parser. Agents write scripts: cd web && npm ci && npm run build 2>&1 | tail. You need pipes, lists, cd tracking, redirects, heredocs, bash -c "…", and wrappers like sudo, env, timeout, xargs, npx and python -m. Knowledge of what tools do behind the scenes. Which hosts cargo build reaches, where uv keeps its cache, which pnpm subcommands start a server. Restraint. Generalize a write to the cache folder, never to your home folder. Treat tools that need your credentials (gh, docker, git push over SSH) as "run outside the sandbox", not "punch a hole in it". I built sandfit to do this. Measure before you switch The most useful thing a tool like this can do is tell you what will break before you change anything. sandfit replays your history against the sandbox you have today, and against the policy it proposes. To keep that number honest, it builds the policy from your older history and tests it on your newest 20%, which it never looked at. A policy that only fits the data it was built from is easy; one that works on next week's commands is the point. Here is what that looks like on a sample week of Next.js work (sample data, shipped in the repo's demo/ folder): If you turn on the sandbox today ███████░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░ 28% of your shell commands would break (69 of 243) With the sandfit policy ░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░ 0% would break (0 of 49 commands from your newest 20% of history, which the policy never saw) 2 commands that read secrets are blocked on purpose Manual approvals you would no longer need: 24 of 35 The files a hijacked agent goes for In July 2026, Pillar Security escaped the sandboxes of Cursor, OpenAI's Codex, Google's Gemini CLI and Antigravity, without breaking the sandboxes themselves. The agent wrote files that a trusted tool outside the sandbox later acted on: hook configs, IDE task files, git metadata. That is the important lesson for anyone configuring a sandbox: the dangerous permission isn't "write anywhere", it's "write to a file something else will execute later". So whatever your history says, a good policy always denies writes to: git hooks and .git/config (which can point hooks at any script) shell startup files (~/.zshrc, ~/.bashrc, …) .mcp.json and editor task configs (.vscode) the agent's own settings, so it can't loosen its own sandbox And it always denies reading credentials: ~/.ssh, ~/.aws, ~/.npmrc, .env files. (Earlier in 2026, a prompt injection against Cline's GitHub triage bot ended with stolen npm publish credentials and an unauthorized release.) Don't trust the forecast, test it I didn't want to publish "trust me" numbers, so sandfit is tested against a real sandbox. The test suite builds a policy from a small history, then runs probes inside sandbox-runtime (bubblewrap on Linux, Seatbelt on macOS): things the history needed, and attacks like reading a planted fake SSH key, editing ~/.zshrc, writing a git hook or reaching an unknown host. Then it compares what the real sandbox did with what sandfit predicted. Writing that test found real bugs. The srt config was missing allowLocalBinding, so dev servers broke on macOS. A mv build.zip ~/Downloads/ granted all of ~/Downloads. Linux and macOS disagree about whether a sandboxed process can bind a local port. All fixed, and all now covered by tests that run on both systems in CI. Try it npx sandfit # read-only: what breaks today, what breaks with the policy npx sandfit explain # why each rule is there npx sandfit apply # write it (asks first, keeps a backup) It runs entirely on your machine and works with Claude Code, Codex, sandbox-runtime and nono. The code, benchmarks and real-sandbox tests are at github.com/hardikverma22/sandfit. If it gets something wrong on your history, open an issue; I want to hear about it. Repo: https://github.com/hardikverma22/sandfit · try it with npx sandfit

articles.title: Rethinking Hexagonal Architecture with Elegant Objects
articles.description: Hexagonal architecture provides a useful foundation: business behavior should remain independent of the technologies used to expose it or persist its state. Ports define the interactions; adapters connect them to the outside world. Yet this separation does not, by itself, tell us where behavior belongs. One common implementation keeps the dependency directions of hexagonal architecture but puts most business decisions in use cases and services. Domain objects then act mainly as data structures, while other objects interpret and change their state. That is a valid design in some contexts, but it is not the only way to apply hexagonal architecture. Reading Elegant Objects challenged how I approached this design. Its emphasis on encapsulation, composition, and small objects led me to ask: what changes when domain objects own more of the behavior that depends on their state? I will explore that question through an e-commerce cart. The examples are deliberately small: supporting types and repetitive delegation methods are omitted. Start with the responsibility The usual suspects A common implementation of “add an item to the cart” might distribute the work across: AddItemToCartUseCase, a port, and its implementation; CartController, a primary adapter that receives AddItemRequestDto; CartRepository, a secondary port, and JpaCartRepository, its adapter; CartEntity, the JPA model, and Cart, the domain model, connected by CartMapper; CartDto, which carries the response. This can involve around ten types for one operation. Each can have a legitimate purpose. A persistence model may protect the domain from ORM constraints. A DTO may define a stable API contract. An application service may coordinate objects and transactions. The design becomes harder to follow when those types divide one concept's behavior among them. For example, Cart may expose data while a use case decides what that data means and how it can change. Hexagonal architecture does not require this arrangement. It permits a rich domain model. The question is whether our implementation makes that model visible. Before adding another layer, I want to establish what a cart is responsible for. Give the cart an explicit contract For this example, a cart knows its contents and total. It can accept or remove an item and initiate checkout: public interface Item { String sku(); Money price(); } public interface Items { Iterable<Item> all(); Item item(String sku); public interface Cart { Items items(); Money total(); void add(Item item); void remove(Item item); Order checkout(Payment payment); The examples below omit repetitive methods such as remove() and checkout(), along with error handling and transaction boundaries. The caller asks the cart to perform an operation. It does not retrieve a mutable list, modify it, and ask a repository to save the result. This gives the cart a boundary for rules about its contents. The distinction goes beyond method names. Renaming getTotal() to total() changes little if the calculation still lives elsewhere. What matters is that the cart owns the meaning of its total and hides how it is obtained. The contract exposes the values needed by callers through sku() and price(), while keeping cart operations behind its own boundary. Each item represents one cart entry. Quantities, discounts, and price changes belong in explicit concepts such as a CartLine. checkout() makes the cart responsible for coordinating payment and order creation. An application service can coordinate the wider workflow, while the cart owns rules about its contents. Keep persistence behind the contract Once the behavior is defined, we can choose how to implement it. Here, PgCart represents a user's cart stored in PostgreSQL: public final class PgCart implements Cart { private final DataSource db; private final long user; public PgCart(final DataSource db, final long user) { @Override public void add(final Item item) { new JdbcSession(this.db) .sql("INSERT INTO cart_item (user_id, sku) VALUES (?, ?)") .set(this.user) .set(item.sku()) .insert(Outcome.VOID); The constructor captures the dependencies and the cart's identity. Database work happens when an operation is invoked. This implementation removes the need for a separate persistence entity and its mapper in this example. PgCart encapsulates access to persistent state and exposes it through the Cart contract. It is not a persistence-ignorant domain object: it combines domain behavior with database access, and a call such as items() may involve database queries. One important distinction: its fields are final, but the cart's observable state can change. Adding an item changes the database, and a later call may return different contents. Fixed references do not make a persistent object an immutable value, nor do they guarantee thread safety. The Cart contract knows nothing about SQL or DataSource, and PgCart depends on that contract. Cart is a domain abstraction, not an application port. PgCart is both a secondary adapter and a domain object: the dependency points inward, but domain behavior and persistence are deliberately combined. The hexagon remains at the system boundary: TkCart translates HTTP requests, and PgCart connects the cart to PostgreSQL. Inside that boundary, this design keeps the domain abstraction and persistence behavior together rather than introducing a separate persistence port. The roles in this example are: TkCart is the primary HTTP adapter. JsonCart defines the JSON representation. Cart, NonEmptyCart, and LoggedCart form the domain contract and its decorators. PgCart is both the secondary PostgreSQL adapter and a domain object. FakeCart is a test implementation of Cart. Compose behavior around the object With a behavioral interface in place, additional responsibilities can be expressed through composition. Suppose checkout must reject an empty cart. A decorator can make that rule explicit: public final class NonEmptyCart implements Cart { private final Cart origin; public NonEmptyCart(final Cart origin) { public Order checkout(final Payment payment) { return this.origin.checkout(payment); We can then assemble the cart where the application's dependencies are wired: new LoggedCart( new NonEmptyCart( new PgCart(db, user) ), log ) The composition shows which responsibilities apply: persistent storage, an empty-cart check, and logging. Each wrapper depends on Cart, so its behavior can be tested with a small fake implementation such as FakeCart. Order matters: logging surrounds validation and records rejected checkout attempts as well as successful ones. The empty-cart check and checkout are separate calls, so another request could modify the cart between them. PgCart must enforce the invariant atomically with the relevant database changes. A real checkout must also account for payment failures and retries. A database transaction cannot atomically include an external payment provider. Moving behavior into objects makes these responsibilities easier to locate, but does not remove them. Give HTTP representation its own responsibility The next boundary is the API response. The domain should remain independent of HTTP and JSON libraries. The Takes framework's RsJSON example provides a useful starting point: a response wraps an object capable of producing JSON. I use that approach through a dedicated representation object, keeping framework dependencies outside the Cart contract. public final class JsonItem implements RsJSON.Source { private final Item item; public JsonItem(final Item item) { public JsonObject toJSON() { return Json.createObjectBuilder() .add("sku", this.item.sku()) .add("price", this.item.price().toString()) .build(); public final class JsonCart implements RsJSON.Source { private final Cart cart; public JsonCart(final Cart cart) { final JsonArrayBuilder items = Json.createArrayBuilder(); .add("total", this.cart.total().toString()) .add("items", items) JsonCart owns the response structure. It wraps a cart instead of copying its values into a second model before serialization. Formatting money as a string keeps this example short; a public API may need separate amount and currency fields. The HTTP entry point wires the same decorators around the persistent cart before returning the representation: public final class TkCart implements Take { private final Logger log; public TkCart(final DataSource db, final Logger log) { public Response act(final Request req) throws Exception { return new RsJSON( new JsonCart( new PgCart(this.db, new UserOf(req).id()) ); TkCart receives the shared database connection and logger when it is constructed. For each request, it extracts the user's id, builds the same LoggedCart(NonEmptyCart(PgCart(...))) composition, and wraps it in the JSON representation. The HTTP adapter connects request identity, cart behavior, and response without making the domain contract depend on HTTP. The response would look something like this, with illustrative prices for IT books about Elegant Objects and hexagonal architecture: This gives the API representation a clear place to evolve. A different response format can be introduced without changing Cart. The mapping responsibility still exists; it now belongs to an object that produces the representation directly. An alternative is to pass the result of Json.createObjectBuilder() to a mapToJson method on Item and Cart. Each object would then choose which parts of its state to expose, at the cost of coupling business interfaces to the JSON API. Here, JsonItem and JsonCart keep that representation responsibility outside the domain contract. A DTO remains useful when an explicit snapshot is required. In this example, items() and total() are separate reads, so concurrent changes could produce an inconsistent response. A DTO alone does not solve that problem; the implementation needs a consistent read strategy or snapshot if the API promises that both describe the same instant. Use names to communicate responsibility Some naming rules of thumb I now follow: Prefer names that say what an object is. Names ending in -er, such as Controller, Mapper, Manager, or Handler, describe what an object does to others. They point toward procedures organized around someone else's data. Prefer the underlying concept: Payment, Outbox, or Cart. Use technology prefixes to distinguish implementations. PgCart identifies the PostgreSQL implementation; TkCart and RsJSON identify framework-facing objects. StripePayment is clearer than CardPayment when naming an implementation tied to a payment provider. In a codebase using Takes, Fk already means Fork (FkRegex, FkTypes), while Takes calls its test doubles RqFake and RsFake; FakeCart avoids giving one prefix two meanings. Prefixes help only when the team shares their meaning. Use adjectives to describe decorators. NonEmptyCart and LoggedCart make added behavior visible; CachedItems would communicate the same idea for a cached collection. The other names in this example follow the same intent: Cart defines the business contract, JsonCart identifies an API representation, and FakeCart provides a test implementation. Evaluate the trade-offs The main benefit of this experiment is a more direct relationship between a business concept and its behavior. We can find cart operations through Cart, persistence through PgCart, and response formatting through JsonCart. This does not guarantee fewer classes. Decorators and representation objects can increase their number. The useful measure is how much of the system a developer must understand to change a rule safely. Several constraints deserve attention: Data access: small objects can hide repeated queries. Measure query behavior and choose batching or a deliberate loading strategy. Caching requires a clear lifetime and invalidation policy. Consistency: composition does not define transaction boundaries. Business invariants must hold under concurrent access and partial failure. Testability: FakeCart lets tests exercise decorators such as NonEmptyCart without infrastructure. PgCart owns database-backed behavior, including total(), so tests of those rules require PostgreSQL. This design makes some behavior easy to test in isolation; it does not make the persistent cart infrastructure-free. Framework integration: frameworks built around mutable entities, reflection, and generated mappings may make this approach costly to introduce. Navigation: many small objects can reduce local complexity while making the overall behavior harder to follow. Shared conventions and selective decomposition matter. For an existing application, start with one bounded behavior and assess the result: can the team locate the rule more easily, test the right boundary, and understand the dependencies? Those answers provide better guidance than adherence to a naming rule or a target class count. Bring the question back to your code Choose a business concept in your application: a cart, an invoice, or an order. Follow one operation from the entry point to persistence and identify where each decision is made. Does the object own its rules, or must its callers understand its internal state to apply them? When a decision depends on the object's own state, moving it behind the object's contract can strengthen encapsulation. When an operation coordinates several objects or external systems, an application service may still be the clearest place for that coordination. Hexagonal architecture helps us control the boundary between the application and its environment. Elegant Objects encourages us to examine the responsibilities within that boundary. Together, they offer a useful way to question familiar structures and make design choices explicit. The goal is a system whose behavior can be located, understood, and changed with confidence.

articles.title: The Ipromptism Checklist: 7 Habits to Stay Literate with AI
articles.description: A few months ago I published Ipromptism: Is AI Creating a New Form of Illiteracy?. The idea was simple: we are learning to prompt faster than we are learning to think with AI. We can get a fluent answer in seconds, yet many of us are losing the ability to judge, verify, or rebuild that answer ourselves. I call this pattern Ipromptism (the framework is archived on Zenodo: 10.5281/zenodo.23212581). The most common reaction I got was: "OK, I recognise the problem. Now what do I actually do on Monday morning?" This post is my answer. Why a checklist? I have trained more than 2,500 people on AI tools, from developers to managers to people who had never opened ChatGPT. One thing comes up in almost every session: awareness alone does not change habits. People nod at the concept and then go back to copy-pasting the first output they get. Checklists work because they are boring in the best way. Pilots and surgeons use them because good intentions break down under pressure. Shipping code with an AI assistant at 6 p.m. on a Friday is exactly that kind of pressure. So here are seven habits I recommend to builders who want to use AI heavily without outsourcing their thinking. The Ipromptism checklist 1. Write the goal before you write the prompt Before you open the chat window, write one or two sentences in your own words: what problem am I solving, and what does "done" look like? If you cannot state the goal without the AI, you are not ready to prompt yet. Keep this note next to your prompt. It becomes your yardstick for judging the output. This one habit turns the AI from an oracle into a tool you are steering. 2. Predict the answer first Take thirty seconds to guess what a good answer should contain: the approach, the main risk, the rough shape of the code. If the output matches your prediction, you have gained confidence. If it does not, you have learned something, or caught a mistake. Either way, you stay an active participant instead of a passive reader. 3. Verify, don't vibe Fluent text feels correct. That feeling is not evidence. Run the code. Write or run the tests. Check every API, flag, and library version against the official docs. Hallucinated parameters look perfectly plausible. For factual claims, open the source. If there is no source, treat the claim as a hypothesis. A good rule: the more confident and polished the answer sounds, the more carefully you should check it. 4. Never merge what you can't explain This is the anti copy-paste rule. Before AI-generated code goes into a commit, ask yourself: Could I explain each line to a colleague in a code review? Do I know why this approach was chosen over the obvious alternative? Would I be able to debug it at 2 a.m. without the assistant? If the answer is no, slow down. Ask the AI to explain itself, simplify the solution, or rewrite the tricky part yourself. Code you don't understand is technical debt with a friendly face. 5. Keep the human decisions human AI is great at generating options. Choosing between them is still your job, especially when the choice involves: Security, privacy, or user data Architecture and long-term trade-offs Anything that affects real people (hiring, access, pricing, moderation) Use the AI to widen the set of options and to stress-test your reasoning. Then make the call yourself, and be able to say why. 6. Document your prompts like you document code Good prompts are reusable assets, and bad ones are silent sources of bugs. Save the prompts that work in your repo or team wiki, with a short note on context and limits. Version them when you change models or tools; the same prompt can behave differently. When an AI-assisted change ships, mention it in the PR description. It helps reviewers know where to look harder. Documentation also forces you to understand why a prompt works, which is literacy in action. 7. Teach it forward The fastest way to fight Ipromptism in a team is to talk about it openly. Pair on AI-assisted tasks the way you would pair on code. Share failures, not just wins: the hallucinated function, the subtly wrong SQL, the confident but outdated answer. Help juniors build fundamentals alongside AI, not instead of it. They need to know what good looks like before they can judge what the model produces. A team that discusses how it uses AI will catch more errors than a team where everyone prompts alone. A quick self-check If you want a one-minute version, ask yourself after your next AI-assisted task: Did I write the goal before prompting? Did I verify the output against something real? Could I explain and defend the result without the AI? Three yes answers means you are using AI as an amplifier. If you answered no to any of them, that is exactly where to start. Closing thoughts AI is not making us illiterate by itself. The way we use it can, if we keep trading understanding for speed. The good news is that the fix is not complicated. It is a handful of small, repeatable habits that keep your judgment in the loop. I work on these questions every day as an AI trainer and consultant, with teams and organisations that want to adopt AI without losing their edge. If you'd like to go further, you'll find my workshops, talks, and resources on romainbailleul.fr. I'd love to hear from you: which habit on this list is hardest for you to keep, and what would you add? Let me know in the comments.

articles.title: Our pages have been in the edge cache for twelve days, and the browser is told to cache them for zero seconds
articles.description: Seventy of PubTrivia's 72 public pages are prerendered at build time. The pricing page and the homepage are the two exceptions, because both read the visitor's country to choose a display currency. I went through every response header the site actually sends to find out what a second visit costs, and the answer involves three caches that do not agree with each other about anything. Start with one page, the features index: $ curl -sI https://pub-trivia.app/features | grep -iE 'age|cache|etag|vary|x-nextjs' age: 1052273 cache-control: public, max-age=0, must-revalidate etag: "jkosq8e831r6q" vary: rsc, next-router-state-tree, next-router-prefetch, next-router-segment-prefetch x-vercel-cache: HIT x-nextjs-prerender: 1 x-nextjs-stale-time: 180 Three numbers in there are cache horizons, and they are 1,052,273 seconds, 0 seconds and 180 seconds. 1,052,273 seconds at the edge age is how long the CDN has been holding this exact response. A million seconds is 12.2 days, and it is the same on every prerendered page: across all 70, the median age was 1,032,207 and the highest was 1,059,852. That number is not a cache policy, it is a deployment log. Prerendered output is immutable for the life of a build, so the age of the oldest object tells you when the build happened. Our most recent commit is dated 18 October, the deploy went out the morning of the 19th, and the cache has been serving the same bytes ever since. If you want to know when a Vercel site last shipped and you do not have access to its dashboard, subtract age from date. The two per-request pages are the other extreme: $ curl -sI https://pub-trivia.app/ | grep -iE 'age|cache-control|x-vercel-cache|etag' age: 0 cache-control: private, no-cache, no-store, max-age=0, must-revalidate x-vercel-cache: MISS MISS every time, no-store, age always zero, and no ETag at all. A page that chooses a price from the request cannot be shared between two visitors, so Next marks it private and the CDN is told not to keep it. Over the whole sitemap that is 70 HIT and 2 MISS, every single time I ran it. 0 seconds in the browser max-age=0, must-revalidate means the browser may store the response and may not use it without asking first. Every navigation to a prerendered page, including a reload of a page you read a minute ago, goes back to the network. What makes that cheap is the only conditional-request mechanism we actually have: $ curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{size_download} ' \ -H 'If-None-Match: "jkosq8e831r6q"' https://pub-trivia.app/features 304 0 I did that for all 72 URLs. Seventy answered 304 with a zero-byte body. The other two are the homepage and the pricing page, which have no ETag to send, so the question cannot be asked and the full page comes back every time. The ETags are short. Of the 70, 55 are 16 characters, 10 are 17, and 5 are 15, all of them strong (no W/ prefix) and all of them opaque: a content hash, not anything you can read a date out of. Which matters, because the other half of HTTP's conditional vocabulary is missing entirely. Not one of our 72 pages sends a Last-Modified header, so a client that asks politely in the older dialect is simply ignored: -H 'If-Modified-Since: Fri, 31 Oct 2026 00:00:00 GMT' https://pub-trivia.app/features 200 81952 The full 82 KB comes back. There is something slightly absurd about that, because this site does know when each page was last changed and publishes it: every entry in our sitemap carries a lastmod taken from the content registry, which is the date somebody actually revised that page. That date is good enough to hand to a crawler as a freshness signal and it never appears in a response header, where a browser could use it. 180 seconds in the router The third horizon is the one that is not HTTP at all. x-nextjs-stale-time: 180 is Next's client-side router cache, configured in next.config.mjs: experimental: { staleTimes: { dynamic: 30, // Dynamic pages cache for 30 seconds static: 180, // Static pages cache for 3 minutes }, Once you are inside the app, clicking between the guides and the tools and back does not necessarily touch the network, because the router holds the payload for three minutes. The thing it holds is not the HTML: $ curl -sI -H 'RSC: 1' https://pub-trivia.app/features | grep -iE 'content-type|x-vercel-cache' content-type: text/x-component That is the React Server Components payload for the same route, 42,653 bytes against 81,952 for the HTML document, cached separately at the edge and hit just as reliably. It is also exactly what the vary header is for: rsc, next-router-state-tree, next-router-prefetch, next-router-segment-prefetch are four Next-specific request headers, and each combination is a distinct cache entry. The first visit gets a document, every navigation after it gets a component stream, and the CDN keeps both. So the same page has three answers to "how long is this good for": twelve days to the CDN, three minutes to our own router, and nothing at all to the browser's HTTP cache. What compression does to all of it While the probe was running I asked each of the 72 pages for three different encodings. For the whole site: Encoding Total bytes identity 5,081,702 brotli 809,654 That is 6.28 times smaller, and the ratio climbs with page size because our pages share so much structure (one header, one footer, one layout, 72 sets of prose): Page ratio / 150,476 16,801 8.96 /pricing 100,392 12,497 8.03 /quiz-questions/general-knowledge 93,831 12,818 7.32 /legal/cookies 27,052 6,074 4.45 The homepage is the biggest document on the site and compresses the hardest, which is a nice illustration of why "KB of HTML" is a bad metric on its own. It is also the one page that can never be revalidated with an ETag, so those 16.8 KB are paid in full on every visit, by every visitor, including the ones who came back twice in a minute. What I would change The two no-store pages are the only real cost here, and the fix is not to make them static. They are per-request because the price has to be right, and a wrong currency on a pricing page is worse than a slow one. What they could have is a stable ETag of their own: the HTML for a given country and plan set is the same HTML until we change a price, so a hash of the rendered body would let a returning visitor get a 304 instead of 16 KB. Next does not do that for a dynamic route, and doing it by hand means rendering the page to a string before answering, which costs the thing it saves. The Last-Modified gap is cheaper to close and I am going to leave it alone too, on purpose. Adding it would mean every prerendered page claiming a modification date of the build, which is the same wrong signal we deliberately removed from the sitemap when we stopped using new Date() for all 72 entries. A content hash that changes when the content changes is a better answer than a timestamp that changes when the build changes, and we already have one. Check it yourself Everything above is readable from outside, with no account: # how long since we deployed curl -sI https://pub-trivia.app/features | grep -iE '^age|^date' # the conditional request that saves the whole page ET=$(curl -sI https://pub-trivia.app/features | grep -i etag | cut -d' ' -f2 | tr -d ' ') curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{size_download} ' -H "If-None-Match: $ET" https://pub-trivia.app/features # the two pages that are never cached, and have no ETag curl -sI https://pub-trivia.app/ | grep -iE 'cache-control|x-vercel-cache|etag' Then load the pricing page in a browser, because that is the page paying for all of this: it renders per request so that the figure you read is the figure in your own currency. The free tier needs no card, so you can sign up and watch the signed-in half, which is cached by nothing at all.

articles.title: Building a YouTube-only scheduler: per-channel queues, visibility per post, and retries
articles.description: I did not set out to build another social media dashboard. I set out to remove one nightly job: uploading the same finished video, channel by channel, to faceless YouTube channels. What the scheduling engine actually does SocialRoster keeps a separate queue for each channel. A creator uploads a video once, plans it on one calendar, and chooses Public, Unlisted, or Private for that individual post — not for the whole account. The engine then publishes to each connected channel automatically, at the scheduled time, and retries when a publish step fails instead of silently dropping the post. That separation matters. Two channels can share a calendar without sharing a schedule, a visibility setting, or a failure mode. If one channel's publish fails, the others are not blocked behind it. Lessons from shipping YouTube-only First, doing one platform properly beats doing five halfway. The big tools I tried all "support YouTube," but they are built to post everywhere at once and priced that way — often per channel or per social set. A creator running six YouTube channels and nothing else pays for machinery they never touch. Second, the boring constraints are the product. Exact times or a repeatable rhythm, a clear view of what is next, and a local library of finished videos matter more than another analytics chart. Third, the person answering feedback should be the person writing the code. SocialRoster is a new product from an independent maker — me — so trade-offs are visible and fixable, not buried in a roadmap. The story behind it Running faceless YouTube channels sounds passive. Anyone who actually does it knows the unglamorous truth: the videos are the fun part, and the uploading is a second job. Every video has to be uploaded, titled, described, thumbnailed, set to the right visibility, and scheduled, channel by channel. When you run three, four, or six channels, that routine eats your evenings. It ate mine. I work a full-time job, and my channels were supposed to grow on the side. Instead, the side thing had a nightly shift of its own. So I built the tool I wanted. It is called SocialRoster, and it is YouTube-only by design. Upload once — including AI-made videos, which is how a lot of faceless channels produce content now — plan on one calendar, and let it publish automatically. Two plans keep the multi-channel point simple: Starter is $19.99/month for up to 2 channels, and Pro is $29.99/month for up to 6. Both start with a 3-day free trial. If you run faceless or multi-channel YouTube and your current workflow is a calendar reminder and a pile of uploads, I would genuinely like to hear what your process looks like, whether you try SocialRoster or not. — Aaron Colbry, founder Learn more at https://socialroster.dev

articles.title: Next.js Node.js 2FA Login SMS OTP: Evidence Boundaries for US and EU Delivery Records
articles.description: The defensible design for a B2B SaaS compliance notice is an evidence ledger, not a delivery-status dashboard. Keep the login decision, message submission, transport observation, and user action as separate facts. A Next.js or Node.js handler can use the same small adapter for US and EU numbers, but it should never make authentication depend on a polling request completing. This distinction is easy to lose because a single SMS OTP sits in the middle of two workflows. The user needs a short-lived challenge. The compliance team needs a record that explains what the system attempted and what the transport layer reported. Those are related records with different authority. How should a Node.js 2FA login handle SMS OTP evidence? Start with the reviewer’s question: can an engineer reconstruct the decision without opening a messaging console? The application should answer that question from its own events. A provider message reference can support the record; it cannot replace it. For one challenge, record a stable challenge_id, the policy version, creation and expiry timestamps, the destination region needed for policy, and an ordered event sequence. Store a protected verifier rather than the OTP itself. Do not put the full phone number, the code, or message text into routine telemetry. A region label such as US or EU is useful for aggregate analysis; a unique destination label turns an audit field into an expensive metric dimension. The event names should describe observations rather than conclusions: challenge_created, submission_accepted, transport_delivered, transport_failed, challenge_verified, or poll_deadline. submission_accepted means that the adapter accepted a request. transport_delivered means that the messaging path supplied a delivery signal. Neither event proves that a person read the notice or controlled the phone. That is the first invariant. Record Authority Retention purpose Boundary Challenge and verification Authentication service Explain the access decision Atomic expiry and one-time use Submission attempt Application and adapter Explain what was requested Idempotency and retry policy Transport observation Messaging integration Reconcile delivery evidence Unknown states stay unknown User action Application Explain code entry or acknowledgement Never infer it from delivery This split also keeps retention decisions honest. Security decisions and terminal outcomes deserve a defined retention policy. Verbose polling traces do not automatically deserve the same treatment. I count both storage bytes and label cardinality before adding a dashboard field, because a field that is cheap in a log can become costly when copied into a time series. Where should polling stop? Polling is a reconciliation mechanism. It is not a second authentication factor and it is not a reason to hold the login request open. Use a deadline and an interval with jitter. For an illustrative policy, a 10-minute challenge lifetime and a 30-second reconciliation window give the user room to complete a normal login while preventing a worker from waiting indefinitely on a carrier path. Those values belong in configuration with an owner and policy version; they are not protocol constants. The worker should persist every meaningful observation, stop on a terminal state, and write an explicit poll_deadline when the deadline wins. The login handler can return a generic response after it has persisted the challenge and submission attempt. Verification then checks the protected challenge record, its expiry, and its one-time-use state. A delayed delivery update may improve the audit trail or user experience later, but it must not retroactively authorize a login. The adapter boundary can be expressed without binding the application to a commercial API: curl --request POST \ --url https://messaging.example.internal \ --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \ --header 'Idempotency-Key: challenge-7f1c' \ --data '{"channel":"sms","purpose":"login_otp","to":"+1XXXXXXXXXX","text":"Your sign-in code expires soon."}' The returned message reference belongs in the attempt record. It does not belong in a high-cardinality metric label. A small counter grouped by channel, outcome, region, and policy version is generally more useful for operations than a unique series for every message. Which failures belong to which owner? The failure taxonomy should be decided before the code is deployed. A rejected destination is a delivery outcome. An incorrect code is an authentication outcome. A worker restart is a reconciliation failure. A user who requests another code triggers a new attempt that must remain linked to the original challenge or explicitly create a new challenge according to policy. For US and EU traffic, normalize the destination at the integration boundary and retain only the regional fact required for policy and reporting. Test invalid numbers, unsupported destinations, delayed observations, duplicate callbacks, replayed callbacks, and worker restarts. Regional sender requirements and routing behavior can change, so configuration needs an owner and a review path rather than a hidden conditional in a request handler. An unknown status is a valid state. Converting “no callback observed” into “failed” creates a claim the system did not establish. Conversely, labeling a submission as delivered because the request returned successfully creates false compliance evidence. The audit record should preserve both the observed state and the time at which the application stopped waiting. How should the system be tested and operated? The test suite should exercise the event ledger, not just a happy-path controller test. Assert that a duplicate submission is idempotent, that a challenge cannot be used twice, and that a late callback cannot change a completed authentication decision. Replay the same callback twice. Deliver callbacks out of order. Kill the reconciliation worker between reading a status and committing the event. The resulting record should remain explainable. Operational telemetry needs a separate budget. Keep every security decision and terminal outcome required by the audit policy. Sample repetitive polling logs after the event schema is proven, and aggregate metrics by bounded dimensions. A unique provider reference is valuable for lookup in structured logs, but it is a poor metric key. This is where observability becomes governance: less retained detail can be the more accurate design when the discarded detail is redundant and the retained event is authoritative. Email has the same evidence boundary. Sender authentication and delivery guidance can affect acceptance, yet an accepted message is not a read receipt. The channel changes; the record model does not. This design has a real limitation: an append-only ledger, bounded polling, and regional policy metadata require more schema and review work than one mutable status field. A small internal tool with no compliance obligation may reasonably omit that burden. A B2B SaaS login tied to an auditable notice should accept the extra state because the simpler design cannot explain retries, late observations, or the authentication decision. What should be rejected in review? Reject a design with one mutable status column as its only history. Overwriting accepted with delivered erases ordering, duplicate attempts, and the difference between an observation and a decision. A current-status read model is useful for a support screen, but it should be derived from an append-only event trail. Also reject any design that makes a carrier lookup part of the authorization critical path. It couples login latency to a transport system that cannot prove human possession. The appropriate decision rule is narrower: authenticate from the short-lived challenge; use transport observations to reconcile the compliance notice; retain enough context to explain the policy and outcome; and keep secrets out of the evidence stream. That boundary is the architecture decision. It makes the integration replaceable, the audit record legible, and the telemetry proportionate to what it can actually prove. References Google, “Email sender guidelines”: https://support.google.com/a/answer/81126 Twilio, “SMS documentation”: https://www.twilio.com/docs/sms OWASP, “Authentication Cheat Sheet”: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.html RFC 6238, “TOTP: Time-Based One-Time Password Algorithm”: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6238 MDN, “HTTP response status codes”: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status

articles.title: 👻 Ghost Terminal: A Ghost Living Inside Your Terminal
articles.description: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine What I Built What if your terminal wasn't just a place where you execute commands, but a place where a ghost lives? Introducing Ghost Terminal – an AI-powered command-line companion that brings a little Halloween spirit into everyday programming. The idea is simple: imagine running a command and having a mysterious ghost respond with spooky, humorous, and sometimes surprisingly intelligent commentary. For example: $ mkdir haunted_house 👻 THE GHOST: "Another house for the forgotten... I wonder what secrets you'll hide inside." Ghost Terminal observes terminal commands, understands their context, and responds with its own spooky personality. I interpreted the theme Ghost in the Machine quite literally: a ghost inhabiting the machine we use every day as developers – the terminal. Instead of building another ordinary chatbot, I wanted to experiment with bringing AI directly into the developer's command-line environment. The project is open source, and contributions are welcome! How I Built It I built Ghost Terminal using Python and an open-source AI ecosystem. Technology Stack: Python: Core application logic and command-line interaction. Ollama: Runs open-weight language models locally. Llama / Qwen: Provides the intelligence and personality behind the ghost. Rich: Makes the terminal experience more interactive and visually appealing. Subprocess: Captures command execution and output. How it works: The user enters a terminal command. Ghost Terminal executes the approved command. The application captures the command and its output. The captured context is passed to a locally running AI model. The model generates a spooky, context-aware response. The ghost speaks directly in the terminal. The AI is designed to observe and comment on commands rather than independently execute potentially dangerous actions. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? For Ghost Terminal, open innovation is not just a technology choice; it is the foundation of the project. Using open-weight models and local inference through Ollama gives the project several advantages: Privacy: Commands and their output can remain on the user's machine instead of being sent to an external AI API. Offline capability: Once the model is downloaded, the application can work without an internet connection. Model flexibility: Developers can experiment with different open-weight models instead of being locked into one provider. Accessibility: No mandatory paid AI API subscription is needed for local inference. Customization: The ghost's personality, behavior, and responses can be modified according to the developer's preferences. A closed AI API could provide similar conversational capabilities, but local inference gives developers greater control over where their data goes and how their AI behaves. That is what makes open innovation exciting: we are not simply using AI; we have the freedom to experiment with it, modify it, and build something of our own. The Spirit of It Halloween is usually associated with haunted houses, mysterious sounds, and things hiding in the dark. But as developers, we spend a lot of time inside a different kind of dark place: the terminal. I wanted to bring a little personality into that environment. Maybe the next time a developer runs a command, they won't just see its output. They might hear a little whisper from the machine itself. Because sometimes, the biggest mystery isn't what is inside your computer. It's what is living inside your terminal. 👻 Prize Categories Open-Source AI Local / Offline AI Thanks to the Hacktoberfest community for creating opportunities to experiment, build, and learn with open-source technology! The machine is awake. Are you ready to talk to it? 👻

articles.title: Make GitHub Actions OIDC trust depend on the claims you can enforce
articles.description: Make GitHub Actions OIDC trust depend on the claims you can enforce GitHub Actions can obtain a short-lived OpenID Connect token and exchange it for cloud access without storing a long-lived cloud secret in the repository. The convenience shifts the security question to the trust policy outside GitHub. That policy must decide which token subjects and audiences are allowed to assume which role. The subject is a scoped statement GitHub documents the OIDC token's subject and audience claims as the values a cloud provider checks against a preconfigured trust definition. The default subject can identify the repository and context, and organizations can customize the format to require claims such as job_workflow_ref. A custom audience can also be supplied when an action needs one. The subject is not merely a repository name. Different workflow triggers can produce different subject claims, so a policy that accepts a broad pattern may include workflows the role owner did not intend. Pull request workflows, branch workflows, environment jobs, and reusable workflows can carry different context. Review the actual claim for each trusted path. GitHub provides an OIDC debugger action to visualize claims before integrating a provider. Use a non-production role for that test. A copied example policy is not evidence that the claim format in the organization matches the example. Build a narrow trust policy The cloud trust policy should combine the issuer, audience, subject, and any provider-specific conditions that distinguish the intended workflow. Require the repository owner and repository identity, not just a human-readable name. Where the provider supports immutable repository identifiers, use them to reduce the effect of future renames. Add environment protection rules when a workflow uses an environment. A trust condition that references an environment is stronger when the environment has reviewers or deployment restrictions. Otherwise the claim identifies a context that any eligible workflow may be able to request. Separate deployment roles by environment and purpose. A production deployment role should not be assumable by every branch or every pull request workflow. A read-only inventory job should not receive a role that can change infrastructure. The cloud provider's session policy can narrow the exchange further. Watch for workflow-level changes The trust policy can remain unchanged while a workflow change expands who can obtain a token. A new permissions block, a new reusable workflow, a changed branch protection rule, or a new environment reviewer can alter the path. Treat those changes as security-sensitive. Review actions that receive the OIDC token. A third-party action with unnecessary token access can exchange it for credentials if the trust policy permits its subject. Pin actions to reviewed versions, limit workflow permissions, and avoid passing tokens into steps that do not need them. The token itself is short lived, but the cloud session it creates may outlive the job. Log the assumed role and the token claims that the provider accepted. Do not log the token. Alert on a new subject assuming a sensitive role, an unexpected audience, or a role assumption from a workflow that normally has no cloud access. Test the negative cases Attempt the exchange from an untrusted branch, a workflow without the required environment, a reusable workflow whose subject differs, and a token with the wrong audience. Every case should fail. Then test the intended workflow and confirm the resulting cloud session has only the permissions the job needs. GitHub Actions OIDC reduces standing credentials when the trust policy is precise. The design should make the accepted workflow identity explicit and test the claim values that the cloud provider actually sees. articles.description: Zapier and Make are fine tools, but paying a monthly fee to move a form submission into a spreadsheet stings when you have ten leads a month. A Google Apps Script web app gives you a free HTTPS endpoint that writes submissions straight into a Google Sheet. Here is the whole thing. The endpoint Open a sheet, go to Extensions > Apps Script, and paste: Then deploy it: Deploy > New deployment > type "Web app" > Execute as "Me" > Who has access "Anyone". Copy the URL ending in /exec. The form Any HTML form can post to it: action="YOUR_EXEC_URL" method="POST"> name="name" placeholder="Your name"> name="email" type="email" required placeholder="you@company.com"> type="hidden" name="token" value="change-me"> type="submit">Send Each submission lands as a row: timestamp, name, email, plus two empty columns (status, sent_at) that an auto-reply script can use later. Honest caveats The token in a public page is visible in the source. It stops drive-by bots, not a determined human. For anything sensitive, add real spam protection (a honeypot field helps too). "Anyone" access means anyone with the URL can post. That is the point of a lead form, but do not reuse the same script for private data. Apps Script caps concurrent executions and daily runtime. For ordinary lead volumes you will never notice; for a launch-day spike, test first. Where this goes next Once leads land in the sheet, the auto-reply script from my earlier post answers them within minutes, and the follow-up script bumps the quiet ones after 48 hours. All three pieces - the webhook, the auto-reply, and the follow-up - are packaged with editable email templates and a 10-minute setup guide in the LeadReply Kit. The kit is mock-tested sample code, so read it before pointing it at real leads.

articles.title: I wanted my notes to be plain files, so I built a small Windows notes app (no Electron)
articles.description: Most note apps keep your notes in their own database, or in the cloud behind an account, or they ship a whole web browser inside. I wanted something simpler: plain .md files in a normal folder, links between notes, search, and text that already looks formatted while you type. So I built Leaflet: a free, open-source (MIT) notes app for Windows, written in C# with Avalonia. No WebView, no Electron. How it works Open any folder and every .md file in it (and in subfolders) becomes a note. Nothing is hidden in a database and nothing goes to the cloud, so you can keep the folder in Git, in a synced folder, or on a USB stick. If you rename or move a note, the [[links]] in all the other notes are fixed automatically. What it does Links and backlinks: [[Note]], [[Note#Section]], [[Note|label]], with suggestions as you type [[. The side panel shows which notes link to the current one, its outline and tags. Live preview in the editor itself: the line with the cursor shows raw Markdown, every other line is formatted. Tables, lists, checkbox tasks, footnotes, code, quotes, images, and one note can be embedded in another with ![[Note]]. Search and replace across all notes, #tags like #project/site, and a command palette on Ctrl+P. Safety for your data: autosave, crash drafts, version history with restore, and protection if a file is changed outside the app while you have unsaved edits. Export one note or all of them to HTML and PDF, in the colours of the theme you picked. Three themes (Graphite, Terminal, Light), English and Russian interface, remappable shortcuts. Why Avalonia and not Electron A WebView or Electron app would have given me a Markdown renderer in an evening. It would also have given me a second heavy process and a slower start. Avalonia draws through Skia in a single native process, so Leaflet starts in about a second and uses around 130 MB on a note with 5,000 lines (my measurements, on one machine). PDF export uses SkiaSharp too, so there is no browser anywhere in the app. Try it There is nothing to install: unzip, run Leaflet.exe, pick a folder (Windows 10/11, .NET is included, about 50 MB). It is not code-signed, so SmartScreen may ask you to confirm: "More info" → "Run anyway". What it does not have: plugins, sync, mobile apps. It is a "folder of files" notes app, and anything else you can build on top with Git or a cloud folder. Download: https://github.com/OlegChe77/leaflet/releases/latest/download/Leaflet.zip Source (MIT): https://github.com/OlegChe77/leaflet I'd love to hear what is missing or broken. Issues and comments are welcome.
